Now, I say this is not so; there is a distinct kind of *karpāsa* flower woven into cloth, which is what we call white cotton (*śukla-karpāsa*) today, whereas that made from wool is called coarse serge (*karpaṭa*).
It is four times more refined than the first, its divine virtue is inconceivable, and its value is worth ten billion.
The fifth is its intrinsic nature, which is limpid and clear, termed "fresh white.
The sixth is its essence, which is free from the two obstacles, termed "pure and clean.
These six qualities above represent the sublime function of subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), which pervades the purified life-force; this is termed "upon the coverlet."
The Sūtra says: "There is a great white ox... used to draw the precious chariot.
The commentary states:
These are the characteristics of the ox.
There are four qualities:
first, white oxen;
second, being fat and robust, which means their hides are full and well-fleshed.
Third, physical strength;
fourth, upright beauty.
The Sūtra says: "With many attendants, he went and bestowed equal gifts upon his sons."
The commentary states:
The first half [of the verse] concerns the attendants, and the second half indicates the bestowal.
"Bìn" (儐) is pronounced with the rhyme *bi* and the final *ren* (反); it means a ritual attendant.
The *Yùpiān* states: "It means to guide.
One who goes out to receive guests is called a *bǐn*; one who enters to assist with the rites is called a *xiàng*.
Furthermore, *bǐn* also means to advance or to present; it is sometimes written as *bīn*.
Now, those who precede are called attendants (*bhin*), and those who follow behind are called followers (*cong*).
The characteristics of the chariot described above are the same as those for the pedestrian procession, and they have been fully set forth and enumerated.
As for points that differ from what preceded, they shall be briefly explained according to the text.
Those who read this should provide a detailed word-for-word commentary for each section of the prose; fearing prolixity, I shall stop here.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, these sons arrived at sovereign non-obstruction."
The commentary states:
The fourth [section] concerns the original mind of the Son of Yue.
"Wandering through the four quarters" is a metaphor for transforming the four modes of birth.
One sports because of attaining the awakening of wisdom;
one experiences joy because of attaining the principle of cessation;
and one achieves mastery because of acquiring supernormal powers.
It is unimpeded because it is free from all obstructions.
Alternatively, there are ten kinds of mastery:

first, mastery over wealth; second, mastery over the mind; third, mastery over lifespan; fourth, mastery over karma; fifth, mastery over birth; sixth, mastery over resolve; seventh, mastery over vows; eighth, mastery over supernormal power; ninth, mastery over dharmas; and tenth, mastery over knowledge.
As stated in other places, there are further four masteries: first, mastery over marks;
second, mastery over lands; third, mastery over wisdom; and fourth, mastery over karma.
Now all have been attained.
Regarding the passage from "He addressed Śāriputra" to "the Father of the World," the commentary states:
The first sixty-five and a half verses provide the parables, while the latter eighteen verses provide the application of those parables.
Following the previous structure, this is divided into two parts:
the first eleven verses apply the former provisional teachings, and the subsequent seven verses apply the present ultimate reality.
In summary, there are four provisional [sections]:

first, one verse which correlates the existence of Buddhas throughout the three realms; second, three verses which correlate the perils and deaths of the five destinies; third, five and a half verses which correlate the manifestation of expedient means; and finally, one and a half verses which correlate the avoidance of calamities by relying on these words.
This is the initial passage.
It is the same as the preceding prose section of the sutra, from "all sentient beings" up to "having no heart of wisdom."
The commentary states:
Following this, there are three verses concerning the second section, which collectively address the perils and destruction of the five destinies.
This is divided into three parts:
The first verse corresponds to the vast multitude of people; although the various sons living there who lack noble lineage are not true sons, they are nonetheless fostered children.
One verse corresponds to the house being dilapidated and decaying.
One verse corresponds to the arising of calamities in all directions.
This is the first passage.
"Deeply attached to worldly pleasures" means that the arising of evil is profound.
There is also a version that reads "deeply attached to the five desires," but taking the former as correct is appropriate because it applies universally to all three realms.
There is no mind of wisdom, nor is there any benevolent intent.
Regarding the scripture’s passage, “In the three realms there is no peace; they burn with unceasing intensity,” the commentary states:
The first verse describes how the dwelling is dilapidated and decaying;
likewise, the five aggregates are all oppressed by the four types of suffering, subject to transience and transformation.
The final verse describes how calamities arise from all directions; throughout the four stages of birth, old age, sickness, and death, the fierce fire of afflictions blazes intensely.
The character "chì" (熾) is pronounced with the initial *zhì* and means "flourishing.
Regarding the sutra passage, "The Tathāgata has already departed [from the world] and dwells in peace within the forest wilds," the commentary says:
The third section below consists of five and a half verses, which collectively demonstrate the application of skillful means (*upāya*).
It is divided into three parts:

the first three verses collectively show the arising of compassion through the vision of suffering; the next one verse collectively shows the great [Bodhisattva] who has no expectations; and the final one and a half verses collectively present the formal teaching of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*).
Only through non-conceptualization can one be delivered.
This section further has three parts:
the first verse clarifies leaving one's own home; the second verse clarifies that the home belongs to oneself; and the third verse clarifies one's own capability.
This is the first [point].
It is tranquil because it realizes nirvana; it is secluded because it emerges from birth-and-death.
It is constantly in meditative concentration because it is profoundly expansive and free.
"To dwell securely in the forest" means that it is indeed a grove of meritorious qualities. As a verse says:
"The elephant king dwells in the wilderness, / Roaming freely with a mind free from sorrow; / The wise person dwells in the mountain forests, / Rejoicing in the bliss of carefree tranquility."
The Sūtra says: "Now, these three realms... are all my children.
The commentary states:
The house belongs to me; those born within it are all my children.
The Sūtra says: "And now, this place is able to provide rescue and protection.
The commentary states:
This clarifies that one possesses one's own power and capability; it is not the power of others.
Regarding the sūtra passage, "Although he provides instruction, it is because his attachment is profound," the commentary states:
One verse collectively demonstrates the absence of great aspiration.
"Jiao" (Teaching) means instruction;
"zhao" (Edict) means clarification.
Although they were thus instructed and clarified, they did not believe in the Mahāyāna because their indulgence in desire was profound.
Some say it is "instruction and inducement" (*jiaozhao*); "inducement" (*zhao*) means to entice, because it clearly guides and instructs.
As the Sūtra says: "Therefore, by means of skillful means, [one attains] the supramundane path."
The commentary states:
This summarizes the correct teaching of the three vehicles.
It refers to the passage in the sutra from "these sons" up to "bodhisattvas who have reached non-retrogression."
The commentary states:
The fourth section concerns avoiding calamity by relying on words.

One whose mind is resolved does not doubt the Four Truths and attains realization of the Ultimate Truth; one who possesses the six supernormal powers becomes an Arhat, while the other two fruits may be understood accordingly.
The treatises state that from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, those who dwell in the stage of non-retrogression have transcended birth within the realm of segmented existence (*paricchinna-jāti*).

As for the three types of higher knowledge (*vidyā*): the higher knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-vidyā*), the higher knowledge of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-vidyā*), and the higher knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vidyā*). These enable one to know, respectively, the past, the future, and the present, thereby eliminating ignorance regarding the three temporal limits (*traiyadhvika-sammoha*).
Because their objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are supreme, these three alone are called "illuminations" (*vidyā*).
Regarding the Sūtra passage: "O Śāriputra, until you attain the Buddha-way," the commentary says:
Below are seven verses; these verses collectively explain the actual [teaching].
This section is divided into two parts:
the first two verses show that the father gave only one [gift], while the latter five verses praise the excellence of the vehicle's virtues.
This is the first [section].
Regarding the Sūtra’s statement, “This vehicle is subtle and wondrous, reaching the state of being unsurpassed,” the commentary says:
The five verses praise the superior virtues of the Vehicle (yāna).
This is divided into four parts:

the first verse praises the four virtues of the Vehicle; the next verse praises it as extolled by the noble ones; the following verse praises it as an instrument of enjoyment; and the final two verses praise it as the supreme bliss.
This is the first [point].
It possesses four virtues:

first, because it is subtle, profound, and supreme; second, because it is pure and free from hindrances; third, because it is the foremost and most excellent; and fourth, because it is unsurpassed and nothing can exceed it.
The Sūtra says: "From that which is approved by the Buddha up to making offerings and prostrations.
The commentary states:
"That which is praised by the Sage."
Not only does the Buddha rejoice and praise this, but it may also serve as that toward which the three karmas of sentient beings all turn in devotion.
As the Sūtra says: "From immeasurable billions... up to the remaining dharmas of the Buddha."
The commentary states:
This verse praises the instruments of enjoyment.
The Sūtra says: "Having obtained such a vehicle, one proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment."
The commentary states:
This praises the joy of the first [stage].

Regarding the phrase "constantly enjoying play throughout the kalpas of day and night," it means that once those of the three vehicles have ascended together to the first bhūmi and above, they ride upon this single vehicle of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) and reach the stage of Buddhahood only after two asaṃkhyeya-kalpas.
If those of the two vehicles ride upon the untainted teachings and the tainted vehicle, they enter the first stage only after one great asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
Such is the general designation for the reckoning of days, nights, and kalpas.
Because the three types of mind-made bodies ride upon this single vehicle of the untainted jewel, they proceed directly to the stage of Buddhahood at the site of enlightenment.
The place where the aggregates of bodhi and nirvāṇa arise is called the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).

Alternatively, because one rides upon the causal vehicle of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), one reaches the site of great parinirvāṇa within the stage of Buddhahood; or else, one reaches the site of the Buddha-fruit suchness (*tathatā*).
This refers to the causal vehicle (*hetu-yāna*), by which one eventually reaches the resultant vehicle (*phala-yāna*).

For this reason, what has been explained above in general terms—that teaching (*śāsana*), principle (*yukti*), practice (*pratipatti*), and fruition (*phala*)—are all the essence of the vehicle (*yāna-svabhāva*).
[The *Sūtra* states: "By these causes and conditions... up to 'except for the Buddha’s skillful means.'"
The commentary states:

This verse summarizes the third major section of the prose, the concluding response: "One should know that by the power of the skillful means of all Buddhas, they distinguish and teach three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle."

Based on the principles explained above, if one seeks with thorough scrutiny throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is no further essence of the two vehicles, except for the Buddha’s skillful means which teach that they exist;
nor is there any further essence of the three ultimate fruits, except for the teaching of their causes through skillful means, which posits three.
Regarding the passage from "He addressed Śāriputra" up to "causing them to exit the triple world," the commentary states:
This correctly illustrates that within the Great Text on Transformation there are three sections.

The preceding section has provided a general summary and indication, answering the reasons for granting the request to speak and correctly explaining the teachings through metaphors to bring about understanding.
From here on, the third section consists of eighty and a half verses, which exhort faith and comprehension in this sutra and inspire joy in the future Buddha-wisdom.
There are two parts:
the first consists of fourteen and a half verses, which reveal that the Dharma has both provisional and ultimate aspects, thereby causing one to abandon the provisional and adopt the ultimate;
the latter consists of sixty-six verses, which demonstrate the right and wrong of persons, thereby causing one to study what is right and eliminate what is wrong.
The beginning and middle sections further consist of two parts:

the first two verses clarify the profound affection between father and son and how one can extract others from suffering; the subsequent twelve and a half verses correctly manifest the provisional and the ultimate, enabling them to adopt and reject accordingly.
This is the first [section].
"Accumulated" (lei) is pronounced with the initial *l* and the final *wei* (li-wei fan). It means to pile up.
From the scripture: "Although I have previously taught... up to 'only the wisdom of a Buddha'."
The commentary states:
The following twelve and a half verses correctly reveal the provisional and the ultimate, causing one to abandon the provisional and grasp the ultimate.
This section contains two parts:

The first one and a half verses provide a general indication of the former as provisional and the present as real; the subsequent eleven verses specifically reveal the present as real and the former as provisional.
This is the first [of those].

Although I previously said that you have attained *nirvāṇa*, this was only because you were able to exhaust that *paricchinna-janma* (segmented birth-and-death) and thereby attain *nirvāṇa*, such that subsequent existence would not continue.

This transformation and rebirth is not brought about by separate karma, for it does not obstruct those beyond training (aśaikṣa) from entering the nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa; therefore, this is omitted here. Your "extinction" (parinirvāṇa) is in fact not the Great Parinirvāṇa, nor is it true extinction.

That which you ought to further cultivate and practice is solely the wisdom of the Buddha: its nature is the Dharma-body and its characteristic is Great Wisdom. Because this wisdom realizes the ultimate principle, the two obstacles do not arise; one thereby attains liberation, termed Great Nirvana, because these three matters are fully perfected.
Regarding the sūtra passage, “If there are bodhisattvas... all are indeed bodhisattvas,” the commentary states:
The following eleven verses concern the present reality and the past expedient means.
This section contains two parts:
the first nine and a half verses clarify that the present is real while the past was provisional, and the final one and a half verses provide a conclusion.
Within the first part, there are further two sub-sections.
The first two verses reveal the present reality, while the subsequent seven and a half verses reveal the past expedient means.
This is the first [of those].
The Sūtra says: "If a person of small wisdom... [up to] there is no difference from the ultimate truth."
The commentary states:
The following seven and a half verses clarify the provisional [teachings] of the past.
This section contains two parts:
The first six verses clarify the provisional Four Noble Truths, while the final one and a half verses explain the attainment of the provisional.
The initial section consists of four parts:

two verses on the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), one and a half verses on the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), one and a half verses on the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), and one verse on the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*).
This is the first [verse].
Regarding the phrase "deeply attached to sensual desire," the beloved internal body and the desired external objects are both the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
The first verse speaks of the Truth of Suffering because its intention is not to abandon conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) in order to enter ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
The subsequent verse states that because sentient beings rejoice, they are able to enter the noble state and attain what has never been attained before.
"Truly without difference" explains that suffering is the truth (*satya*); "truth" carries the meaning of reality.
The *Śālistamba Sūtra* (Sutra on the Bequeathed Teaching) states:
"The Buddha taught the Truth of Suffering; one must not cause it to become pleasant, for it is truly suffering.
The sutra continues: "If there are sentient beings... [up to] ...he teaches the path through skillful means."
The commentary states:
This is the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
"The cause of suffering" refers to the Truth of Origination, which consists of karma and afflictions (*kleśa*).
The "Path" (mārga) is the meaning of cause, which is its very essence;
this is because the Truth of Origination is the cause of the Truth of Suffering.
Furthermore, the Truth of the Path is spoken of because it brings about the cessation of origination.
The Sūtra states: "From 'the cause of all sufferings' up to 'it is called the third truth.
The commentary says:
This is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya).
Greed is the root of suffering, for its origin lies in the arising of suffering;
if the root of greed is extinguished, the fruit of suffering will likewise be extinguished.
That which is "the basis" is the body, which is the fruit of suffering.
To extinguish the accumulation of suffering, the Truth of Cessation is taught.
The Sūtra states: "For the sake of the Truth of Cessation... [it] is called attaining liberation.
The commentary says:
This is the Truth of the Path.
Because one realizes cessation through the path and thereby becomes free from the bonds of suffering,
it is called the realization of nirvana and the attainment of liberation.
Regarding the sūtra passage, "To what extent does this person attain all liberations," the commentary states:
This explains the provisional stage of attainment.
The first two lines pose the question, and the latter four lines provide the answer.

Merely being free from false afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, suffering, and the *paricchinna-jarā-maraṇa* (segmented birth and death) is called attaining liberation, because one has realized the *saṃskṛta-catur-āryasatya* (the four noble truths with conditioned activity). However, one has not yet attained the total extinction of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), the two types of karma, and the two types of death;
this is because all dharmas of liberation are empty, which constitutes the *asaṃskṛta-catur-āryasatya* (the four noble truths without conditioned activity).

There are those who establish the Four Noble Truths as follows: segmented birth-and-death is the truth of suffering; karma and afflictions are the truth of origination; the nirvana with remainder and the nirvana without remainder are the truth of cessation; and the category of wisdom regarding the emptiness of persons is taken as the truth of the path.

Regarding the four truths of non-action: the cycle of birth and death through transformation is the truth of suffering; the cognitive obscuration is the truth of origination; non-abiding nirvana is the truth of cessation; and the category of wisdom regarding the emptiness of phenomena is the truth of the path.
Therefore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states:
"These Eight Noble Truths are not known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
The sūtra further says: "The Buddha speaks of such persons as leading them to ultimate nirvāṇa."
The commentary states:
"To clarify that the present is real and the past is provisional" is the second conclusion of the middle section.
This meaning has two parts:
First, the Buddha taught that those of the two vehicles abide in a provisional state and have not yet attained actual *nirvāṇa*, because these individuals have not yet realized the Unsurpassed Way.
Second, regarding the statement "I also do not wish for those of the two vehicles to abide in the provisional," this refers to their arrival at the *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
He intends to cause them to attain the unsurpassed path of Great Parinirvāṇa, and not to remain in provisional means or ultimate extinction.
As the Sūtra says: "I am the Dharma King... therefore I appear in the world."
The commentary states:

The first fourteen and a half verses clarify the provisional and ultimate aspects of the Dharma, instructing one to abandon the provisional and grasp the ultimate; the subsequent sixty-six verses demonstrate the right and wrong of human conduct, instructing one to study what is correct and eliminate what is erroneous.
This is divided into four parts:
the first two and a half verses clarify that it is because I possess the faculties of wisdom and realization that I am able to speak; "you do not know this, so do not propagate it recklessly.
The subsequent eight verses clarify that those who understand this occupy a high station and have all long planted the roots of virtue.
Next, the first thirty-six and a half verses concern those who lack wisdom and do not believe in the characteristics of sin;
the subsequent nineteen verses should be explained to those who possess wisdom.
Within the former section, there are further two parts:
The first verse explains that my consciousness and faculties enable me to preach; the subsequent one and a half verses state that you do not recognize these and must not propagate them recklessly.
This is the former part.

"Because he is the Dharma King" refers to his general knowledge of both the medicine and the illness; "having mastery over the Dharma" refers specifically to his knowledge of the medicinal Dharma for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings.
Distinguishing the faculties and dispositions of others, he is able to teach in accordance with their capacities; thus, he manifests in the world.
Regarding the passage from the Sūtra, “O Śāriputra, do not propagate this recklessly,” the commentary says:
This clarifies that you do not understand it; do not propagate it recklessly.
"Dharma Seal" (dharmamudrā) refers to the wondrous principle of the One Vehicle, which serves as a seal for the Mahāyāna teachings to ensure their definitive certainty.
I have spoken of this seal for the sake of benefiting others; since you do not recognize either the medicine or the illness, do not transmit it recklessly, lest calamity arise. As the Sūtra says:
"If there are those who hear this, they shall reach the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika)."
The commentary states:
The second section below consists of eight verses. Those who possess faith occupy a high station, having all long planted the roots of virtue.
Among these, there are six verses:

One verse concerns those of superior capacity who are able to believe; one and a half verses concern those who only believe after having encountered the conditions of meeting a Buddha and hearing the teaching in the past; one and a half verses state that if there are those capable of believing what you say, they shall see us; one verse states that those with deep wisdom can believe while those with shallow understanding cannot; one verse concerns those of the two vehicles with fixed lineage who cannot believe; and the final two verses concern those of the two vehicles with unfixed lineage who will subsequently give rise to faith.
This is the first [case].

If there are those who, upon hearing this sutra, give rise to sympathetic joy and honor it with both body and mind, believing in it with the utmost reverence, you should know that such persons abide on the stage of non-retrogression.

*Avivarti* (阿鞞跋致) means "non-retrogression" (*buddha-anivartana*). There are also versions that read *A-vyavartika* (阿惟越致) or *Abhi-vartika* (阿毘跋致); however, *Avivarti* is the correct form, while the others are phonetic corruptions.
Because they are capable of doing so within all four types of non-retrogression—of faith, stage, realization, and practice—and because their faculties and capacities have matured, the Sūtra states:
"If there are those who believe and accept [this], up to 'they shall also hear this Dharma.'"
The commentary states:
Regarding the second [section], it says that those who previously encountered the conditions for meeting a Buddha once heard [the teaching] and now believe because they possess past causes.
As the Sūtra says: "If there are people who can believe in this and all the Bodhisattvas..."
The commentary states:
Thirdly, if one believes what you say, then one sees my body, the bhikṣus, and the bodhisattvas as no different from the Three Jewels, because the Three Jewels are of one and the same essence.
If they were of distinct entities, they would necessarily be perceived, for they would be the cause of perception;
yet we all desire to hear this Dharma, as there is no logical basis for their distinction.
As the Sūtra says: "This Lotus Sūtra reaches even those who are deluded and lack understanding."
The commentary states:
The fourth wisdom is profound and capable of being believed because its principles are deep and subtle.
Those of shallow understanding cannot grasp it; these are referred to as ignorant ordinary beings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*).
The Sūtra states: "Beyond the reach of the powers of all Śrāvakas.
The commentary says:
The fifth [stage] is definitively that which the Two Vehicles cannot realize, as it contradicts their original intention.
One who is not deluded regarding the Dharma may possess faith and integrity, yet lacks compliant practice.
Regarding the Sūtra passage: "O Śāriputra, this reaches beyond the sphere of your own wisdom," the commentary states:
Only those of the sixth class, the indeterminate śrāvakas, are capable of generating faith through gradual stages.
If even you, who possess the highest faculties, must first believe my words before gradually attaining realization, how much more so for others of the indeterminate śrāvaka lineage?
When the Bodhisattva hears this, he is able to contemplate and discern it and enter [into its meaning].
The character "shàng" (尚) has two readings: *cháng* and *liàng*. According to the *Yùpiān*, it is read as *shí liàng*.
It means "perhaps" (*shù*) or "moreover" (*qiě*).
Regarding the passage from "Furthermore, Śāriputra" up to "do not preach this sūtra," the commentary states:
This is the third section below, consisting of thirty-six and a half stanzas, which describes the characteristics of the transgressions of those who lack wisdom and do not believe [in this teaching].
There are two parts:
the first two verses state that if non-Buddhists or ordinary worldlings possess the seven evils, one should not preach to them;
the subsequent thirty-four and a half verses concern those to whom one may preach despite their faults, yet who harbor disbelief regarding the characteristics of the causes and effects of evil.
The beginning has two parts:
the first verse sets forth four faults for which one should not preach, and the second verse sets forth three faults for which one likewise should not preach.
This is the first.
The four evils are:
first, arrogance (*māna*), which is to be intoxicated and dissolute by relying on one's lineage, physical appearance, strength, wisdom, or wealth;
second, pride (*abhimāna*), which is to treat others with contempt through the seven types of pride, such as those of little virtue who claim to have much, numbering five thousand.
Third, those who are indolent, dissolute, and unrestrained, showing no sense of satiety.
Fourth, those with the view of self, such as the followers of external paths.

If they deeply loathe birth and death and joyfully seek transcendence; if they humble themselves before others, respect the Dharma, and apply themselves with diligence without indulgence; if they dispel delusions by contemplating non-self and have faith in and accord with this sutra—only for such persons should it be preached.
Therefore, one should not preach to those who possess these four faults;
the subsequent cases should be understood accordingly.
As the Sūtra states: "To ordinary persons of shallow understanding... do not preach to them either."
The commentary states:
Herein there are three evils:
first, shallow knowledge, which falsely manifests as cleverness and lacks far-reaching discernment.
Second, those who are deeply attached to the five desires, whose bodies and minds are intoxicated by the five desires of household life, and whose afflictions are heavy;
third, foolish and dull ordinary people who lack the spiritual lineage and cannot understand what they hear.
Do not preach this to those of foolish nature, those fixed in their destiny, or those belonging to the two vehicles.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "If there are people who do not believe" up to "the Buddha-seed in the world," the commentary says:
The final thirty-four and a half verses are extracted to explain that they harbor disbelief in the characteristics of the causes and effects of evil.
This section has two parts:
the first four and a half verses concern the planting of evil causes due to disbelief, and the subsequent thirty verses concern the undergoing of evil results due to disbelief.
The first section further has two parts:
the first verse concerns the cessation of goodness due to lack of faith, while the subsequent three and a half verses concern the arising of evil due to lack of faith.
This is the first [of those two].
To extinguish the causes of outflows is called severing the seeds of the mundane world; to extinguish the causes of the outflow-free is called severing the seeds of the Buddha.

By virtue of faith in this sutra, one first perfumes the seeds of mundane wholesome roots, thereby being born among humans and devas to experience superior and wondrous bliss; this nourishes and grows the naturally existing seeds of the outflow-free, after which one gradually enters the state of a noble one.

The newly produced outflows-free [wisdom] develops successively until the fruit of Buddhahood is attained; therefore, believing in this sutra can serve as the proximate cause for humans and devas in the world and the remote cause for attaining Buddhahood, resulting in boundless benefit and joy when one becomes a Buddha in the future.
If one lacks faith oneself, slanders and obstructs [the Dharma], prevents its circulation, or causes others to lack faith, is this not to sever the seeds of both categories?
It is to gouge out and destroy the eyes of gods and humans, or to sever the Buddha-seed of all the world, for it damages and destroys the seeds of the untainted Dharma.

According to this sutra, if there are those who encourage the arousal of the bodhicitta, the lineage of the Buddhas will not be severed; therefore, to slander this sutra is to sever the bodhicitta, which is called severing the lineage of the Buddhas. Because the Dharma is no longer practiced, it is also called severing the lineage of the Dharma. Since one neither arouses the mind nor realizes the noble path, it is also called severing the lineage of the Sangha.
Now, speaking from the perspective of the most prominent [consequence], it is solely the severing of the Buddha-seed.
Regarding the Sūtra passage: "Or again, they frown even upon such a sūtra as this," the commentary says:
The three verses and a half below concern the arising of evil due to lack of faith;
this is twofold:

the first two verses concern the arising of the three types of evil karma through lack of faith in the Dharma, while the latter one verse and a half concern the arising of the four types of evil conduct through lack of faith in persons.
This is the first [point].
"Frowning" (*pin-cu*) refers to a physical sign of lack of faith, such as knitting the brows into a scowl.
Here, the term "frequent" (*pin*) indicates that one repeatedly frowns.
"Bièng" (併) means "to join together"; it refers to the eyebrows being joined in one place.

The commentary states:
Lack of faith toward others gives rise to the four types of evil conduct.
There are four persons toward whom one lacks faith:
first, the reader; second, the reciter; third, the scribe; and fourth, the upholder.
By general principle, one should give rise to a lack of faith toward those who practice these ten types of dharmas;
however, for the sake of brevity here, only four persons are cited as giving rise to the four types of unwholesome conduct.
There are four types of evil conduct:
first, contempt; second, hatred; third, jealousy; and fourth, harboring resentment.
Briefly stated, these four are the causes of the most minor offenses.

In fact, beating and scolding, killing and binding, robbery and plundering, slandering and speaking harshly, as well as anger and malice—all such evils are causes of grave offenses; though they are omitted here, one should listen to their results.
Regarding the sūtra passage, "That person’s life comes to an end and continues until the end of incalculable kalpas," the commentary states:
The following thirty verses describe the characteristics of receiving evil retribution due to lack of faith.
This is divided into two parts:
first, twenty-eight verses clarifying the results of lack of faith; second, two verses forming the conclusion.
Within the first part, there are further two sections:

The first twenty-two verses individually detail the characteristics of experiencing the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) across the three realms of existence; the final six verses collectively detail the characteristics of experiencing the two fruits—the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) and the concordant fruit (*niṣyandaphala*)—across the four realms of existence.
The beginning consists of three sections:

first, one and a half verses on the characteristics of experiencing the retribution of the hells; next, ten and a half verses on the characteristics of experiencing the retribution of animals; and finally, ten verses on the characteristics of experiencing the retribution among humans.
The hungry ghosts (preta) are not mentioned because they are mostly produced by greed, and those who lack faith in this sutra and give rise to greed are few;
thus, they are omitted for brevity, yet they are certainly not absent, as they appear later in the text.
In the first fascicle above, the five destinies were explained through six categories.
Of these, three have already been interpreted:
first, their names; second, their essential nature; and third, their classification and synthesis. These are now concluded.
Now, the remaining three gates will be further distinguished:
first, the location; second, the characteristics of the fruit; and third, the lifespan.
Regarding the location, there are three types of *naraka* (hells):
There are three types: first, the fundamental; second, the neighboring; and third, the solitary.
The fundamental consists of the eight hot and eight cold hells.
As for the eight hot hells:

First, Sañjīva (Reviving); second, Kālasūtra (Black Rope); third, Saṃghāta (Crushing); fourth, Raurava (Crying Out); fifth, Mahāraurava (Great Crying Out); sixth, Tapana (Heating); seventh, Pratāpana (Great Heating); eighth, Avīci (Uninterrupted).
These eight instruments of suffering each occupy a space ten thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth.
As for the eight cold hells:
first, Arbuda; second, Nirarbuda; third, Aṭaṭa; fourth, Hahava; fifth, Huhuva; sixth, Utpala; seventh, Padma; eighth, Mahāpadma.
Thirty-two thousand yojanas below this is the Reviving Hell (Saṃjīva); four thousand yojanas below the Reviving Hell are the Black String Hell (Kālasūtra) and the other six.
Thus, the distance between each of these six hells below is separated by two thousand yojanas.
The eight cold hells are all smaller than the hot hells. These aforementioned are the fundamental hells.
According to one interpretation, the hells are stacked one above the other;
calculating roughly, the distance from the bottom of the Avīci Hell to the earth is one hundred twenty-eight thousand yojanas.
This explanation is incorrect; it is certainly impossible that Mount Sumeru rests upon the golden wheel at a depth of only eighty thousand *yojanas* below the water.

Therefore, another explanation states: "Thirty-two thousand *yojanas* below this [Mount Sumeru] lies the Saṃjīva hell; four thousand *yojanas* further below Saṃjīva lie the remaining seven hells. These seven others are situated side-by-side rather than one above the other.

The first cold hell is level with the Reviving Hell (Saṃjīva). Below the first cold hell are twenty-seven other cold hells; these seven cold hells are also situated side-by-side rather than one above the other.
Each of these eight hells is ten thousand yojanas in breadth, and their vertical dimensions are not specified.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states only: "Below this, there are thirty-two thousand [yōjana] of the Saṃjīva hell; below Saṃjīva, there are four thousand [yōjana] of other *naraka*s.
The first cold hell is situated beside Saṃjīva; below this, there are two thousand [yōjana] of other cold *naraka*s."
"The locations of the *naraka*s are ten thousand [yojanas] wide.
It does not separately state that the distance between the upper and lower [levels] is four thousand each, nor that each individual hell is ten thousand [yojanas].
Therefore, there are two explanations in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.

The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Descending twenty thousand [yojanas] from here to the bottom of the Avīci hell is extremely shallow and near"; this "near boundary" refers to the four gates on each side outside the eight hot hells.

The *Abhidharmakośa* states that there are sixteen additional [hells], namely: the Pit of Hot Ashes (*Kukūla*), the Quagmire of Corpses and Excrement (*Kuṇapa*), the Forest of Sword-leaves (*Asipatravana*), and the River of Boiling Water (*Vaitaraṇī*).
"Solitary" refers to places where one or more individuals suffer punishment, such as mountain ranges, wildernesses, beneath trees, or in the open air.
Beings of the animal realm originally dwell in the great ocean, yet they flow and reside in other places.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states that five hundred yojanas below there is the kingdom of King Yama, from which they subsequently flow to other locations.
Human beings dwell in the four great continents and the eight intermediate continents, each of which has five hundred small islands as its satellites.
Devas dwell in the six heavens of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
The Heaven of the Four Great Kings (Cāturmahārājakāyika) resides on the fourth terrace at the midpoint of Mount Sumeru.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states that they dwell upon the summit of the first golden mountain.
The Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa) dwells upon the summit of Mount Sumeru; all other heavens reside progressively higher in the space above.
The summit of Mount Sumeru is eighty thousand *yojana*s above the earth; all the heavens above it are twice that distance from the ground.

The Yāma Heaven is one hundred and sixty thousand *yojana*s from the earth, and the Tuṣita Heaven is three hundred and twenty thousand *yojana*s from the earth. One should understand that for the heavens from the Anabhraka Heaven upward, the distances follow this same principle.
Because the gods of the formless realm receive their retribution in the desire and form realms according to the place where they previously entered meditative absorption,
these gods do not fundamentally reside beneath the northern ocean on Mount Sumeru.
As for the other minor lateral [realms], they are situated within the four continents as previously described.

Regarding the characteristics of the fruits experienced therein: sentient beings in the hells mostly experience the suffering of extreme punishment; sentient beings among the animals mostly experience the suffering of devouring one another; sentient beings among the hungry ghosts mostly experience the suffering of extreme hunger and thirst; sentient beings in the human realm mostly experience the various sufferings of deprivation and pursuit; and sentient beings in the celestial realms mostly experience the suffering of decline, affliction, and downfall.

Regarding the characteristics of suffering in the eight hot hells: first is the characteristic of suffering in the Reviving Hell (*Saṃjīva*). This refers to when those sentient beings gather together in great numbers, and various instruments of torment produced by the predominance of their karma arise in succession, whereby they inflict mutual injury upon one another until they faint and fall prostrate on the ground.
Next, a great voice resounded from the midst of space, saying:
"These sentient beings may return to the Reviving Hell; they may return to the Reviving Hell!
Thereupon, those sentient beings suddenly rose once more and were subjected again to the remaining tortures of the instruments of suffering as before.
Due to these causes and conditions, they undergo suffering for a long time, until all the evil and unwholesome karma created in previous lives has been exhausted and eliminated.

Second is the characteristic of the Black Rope (Kālasūtra) hell: sentient beings there are for the most part seized by the wardens of that realm, who mark them with black ropes, delineating them into four sides, eight directions, or various patterns and images.

Once they have been cast down, they are subjected to suffering for a long time through various causes and conditions—such as being hewn, split, cut, or pounded at their respective locations; only when their karma is exhausted do they emerge.

Third is the characteristic of suffering through conjunction (*saṃnipāta*): it refers to when those sentient beings occasionally gather and assemble together in turn; at that time, they are then seized by the hell-wardens and driven between two great mountains with iron rams' heads.
Once he has entered, the two mountains press upon him; being thus pressed, blood flows forth from all the openings.
It is the same with the two iron rams, horses, elephants, lions, and tigers.
Furthermore, they are forced together and placed within a great iron vat and pressed like sugarcane; once they have been pressed, blood flows forth.
Having been thus combined, a great iron mountain falls down upon them from above.
They cause those sentient beings to fall upon an iron ground, where they are hacked, pierced, pounded, or torn asunder;
once they have been hacked, pierced, pounded, and torn, their blood flows forth.
They undergo suffering for a long duration, emerging only when their karma is exhausted.
This suffering is threefold:
first, being squeezed between two mountains; second, being crushed by iron rollers; and third, being struck by falling iron mountains.

The fourth is the aspect of wailing in suffering: it refers to those sentient beings who, seeking shelter, enter a great iron chamber; as soon as they have entered, fire breaks out, whereby they are burned, intensely burned, and completely and utterly consumed by flames.
Once they have been burned, they are oppressed by agonizing pain and cry out in lamentation.
They suffer for a long time until their karma is exhausted before they can emerge.

Regarding the five great signs of lamentation and suffering, the distinction from this [previous case] is that while their dwelling is like a womb, because their suffering exceeds what came before, their cries become even louder.

Sixth is the characteristic of the suffering of being scorched by fire: that is to say, those hell-wardens place sentient beings upon great iron cauldrons of threefold heat spanning immeasurable *yojanas*, turning them left and right, and burning them thin on both the surface and the inside.

Furthermore, it is like roasting a fish: using a large iron skewer, one pierces it from below until it emerges from the top, turning it over and over to roast it, causing flames to erupt from all the sense-faculties, pores, and mouths of those sentient beings.

Furthermore, they place sentient beings upon the aforementioned great hot iron ground, either face up or face down, and strike or pound them everywhere with three types of hot, large iron hammers, clubs, or mallets.
They cause them to become like lumps of flesh,
where they suffer for a long duration until their karma is exhausted before they can emerge.
This suffering is threefold:
First, they are scorched and thinned on both sides; second, they are impaled and roasted on iron skewers; third, they are struck and beaten with iron clubs.

Regarding the seventh aspect of the suffering of extreme burning, it differs from the preceding ones in that three large, intensely hot iron skewers are thrust through them from below, passing through their two shoulders and emerging from the crown of their heads; consequently, fierce flames stream forth from their eyes, ears, nose, mouth, and pores.
Furthermore, their bodies are completely wrapped in sheets of red-hot copper and iron, and they are again cast upside down as before.

They are boiled in a great iron cauldron filled with ash-water and the three heats; as the broth surges and boils, these sentient beings are tossed about by the current, sometimes emerging and sometimes submerging, until their flesh, blood, skin, and sinews are entirely dissolved and rotted away, leaving only a skeleton of bones.
They are then filtered out again and placed upon a floor of glowing iron, where their skin, flesh, blood, and veins regenerate as before; they are then returned to the cauldron.
The rest is as described for the Great Hot Hell.
They undergo suffering for a long duration, emerging only when their karma is exhausted.
This suffering is threefold:
first, being pierced by a string of three limbs; second, being bound and wrapped in iron plates; and third, being boiled in hot water.

Eighth, regarding the characteristics of the suffering experienced in the Great Avīci Hell: to the east, upon a great iron ground extending for many hundreds of *yojanas* and heated by three fires, there arise fierce, blazing fire-spikes that surge upward in flames and pierce those sentient beings. They penetrate the skin and enter the flesh, severing the tendons and breaking the bones, further piercing through to the marrow and burning it like a fat candle, until the entire body becomes a mass of intense flames.
In the same way, the fire-spikes in the other directions are likewise.

Consequently, those sentient beings become intermingled with fierce flames; they see only masses of fire approaching from the four directions, with the flames blending together without any interval, and the suffering they endure likewise occurs without interruption.
One hears only the sounds of wailing and crying in pain, thereby knowing that sentient beings exist.

Furthermore, they are made to place iron winnowing baskets filled with three kinds of fiercely blazing iron coals and sift them; then, they are placed upon a floor of hot iron and made to climb a great mountain of hot iron, ascending and descending, descending and ascending again.
They pull out their tongues from their mouths and nail them open with a hundred iron spikes, stretching them until they are free of wrinkles and folds, like stretched ox-hide.

Furthermore, they lay them supine upon the ground of hot iron; using hot iron tongs, they pry their mouths open and place three large, scorching iron balls within. These immediately burn their mouths and throats, passing through the internal organs and exiting from below.
Furthermore, molten copper is poured into their mouths; it burns the throat and mouth, penetrating through to the internal organs, and exits from below.
The remaining suffering is like that of being intensely incinerated.
They suffer for a long duration, emerging only when their karma is exhausted.

This suffering consists of six aspects: first, fire-torches from the four directions; second, being crushed and winnowed by iron coals; third, being pressed between iron mountains above and below; fourth, having one's tongue nailed with iron spikes; fifth, being forced to swallow iron balls; and sixth, having molten copper poured into one's mouth.
This is now a brief explanation of the coarse and manifest instruments of suffering; it does not mean that there are no other instruments of suffering within the great hells.
The above describes the characteristics of the eight primary hot hells.
Regarding the characteristics of the peripheral hells: each individual mahānaraka has four sides, four banks, and four gates.
They are surrounded by iron walls, from which [the fires] issue forth through the four gates.
Outside each of the two gates, there are four gardens:
the first is called the Pit of Hot Ashes (*Kukūla*), where the hot ashes reach up to the knees.

When those sentient beings emerge from their dwellings and wander here seeking shelter, as soon as they set foot down, their skin, flesh, sinews, and bones are instantly consumed and rotted away; yet when they lift their feet, these parts grow back once more.
The second refers to excrement and filth, which form a mire.

When these sentient beings emerge from the former [hell] seeking shelter, they gradually wander about and sink into it until both their heads and feet are submerged. Furthermore, within this mire there are many *śyāmaka* worms; they are one foot in length, with white beaks and black heads. They pierce the skin and enter the flesh, severing tendons and breaking bones to extract and devour the marrow.
Third are the Forests of Razor Blades.
This category is further divided into three:
first, the Road of Sharp Blades, which consists of a path made of sharp-edged swords with their blades pointing upward.

When those sentient beings emerge from that place and wander here, at the moment they set foot down, their skin, flesh, sinews, and bones all dissolve and rot away; yet when they lift their feet, they are restored to their former state.
Second is the Forest of Sword-leaves.

Once those sentient beings have emerged from the former [forest] and approach that thicket, as soon as they sit beneath it, a gentle breeze arises and sword-leaves fall, hacking and severing all their limbs and joints, whereupon they immediately collapse to the ground.
There are black brindled dogs that seize the fetus from its back and devour it.
There are three forests of iron thorns; there is the forest of iron śālmali trees, which resemble the thorny soap-berry tree.

At that moment, there appears a great iron-beaked bird, which perches upon his head or his shoulders, pecking out and devouring the vitreous humor of his eyes.
Fourth is the Garden of the Fierce River.
There is a vast river filled with boiling, hot ash-water.

The hell-wardens immediately pour molten copper into their mouths.
They undergo suffering for a long duration, only emerging once their karma is exhausted.
As for the characteristics of the suffering experienced in the *ekākin-naraka* (solitary hell), although its location is small, it is fully equipped with every variety of instrument of torment.
The characteristics of these are explained in detail in the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchāmahāśvetakuṇḍalakasūtra*.
Regarding the eight cold hells:

first is the Arbuda hell, where sentient beings who have taken birth there are touched by an extremely heavy and vast cold sensation, causing all their limbs and members to contract and shrivel like a boil.
Second is the *Naraka* of Bursting Blisters (*Vipāka*), which is so called because the blisters burst open, pus and blood flow out, and the wounds contract and shrivel.

Third is the *Naraka* of *Kṣuradhāra*, fourth is the *Naraka* of *Hahava*, and fifth is the *Naraka* of *Huhuva*; these three *Narakas* are named according to the distinct sounds of suffering uttered by the sentient beings undergoing punishment therein.

In the sixth hell, the Blue Lotus (Nīlotpala), beings are afflicted by the touch of heavy, vast, and cold suffering; their entire bodies become entirely bluish-black, and their skin cracks into five or six pieces.
The seventh is the Red Lotus (Padma) hell; beyond this Blue Hell, the color changes to red and crimson, and the skin splits apart ten times or more.
The eighth is the Great Red Lotus (Mahāpadma) hell, wherein the bodies are of an extremely large size, red and crimson, and the skin splits apart a hundred times or more.
As for those in the animal realm, they harm one another;
for instance, the weak and frail are slaughtered by the strong and powerful,
undergoing various kinds of suffering.
Lacking self-mastery, they are driven about by others and frequently subjected to flogging; they serve as the means of subsistence for those humans and devas.
Due to these causes and conditions, they undergo all manner of most grievous sufferings.
Briefly, there are three types of beings in the realm of hungry ghosts:
first, those who encounter external obstacles to food and drink; second, those who encounter internal obstacles to food and drink; and third, those for whom there are no obstacles to food and drink.

Regarding those hindered from food and drink by external obstacles: because they practiced extreme stinginess, they are born into the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). They are constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst; their skin, flesh, blood, and veins are all withered like ash and charcoal; their hair is disheveled and matted; their faces are dark and sunken, and their lips and mouths are parched and cracked. They constantly lick their mouths and faces with their tongues, fleeing in terror from place to place in their agony of hunger and thirst.
Whenever they reach a spring or pool, other sentient beings stand in rows guarding it with swords, staves, and lassos, preventing them from approaching.
Or, if they force their way toward it, the spring immediately appears to transform into pus and blood, which they have no desire to drink.
These and others are called those who are obstructed from food and drink by external factors.

As for those obstructed from food and drink by internal factors, it refers to those sentient beings whose throats are like needles, whose mouths are like torches, or who have goiters on their necks and distended bellies.

Due to these causes and conditions, even if one obtains food and drink without other external obstacles, one is naturally unable to eat or drink; such cases as these are called "obstruction of food and drink due to internal factors."

Regarding the Sūtra passage, "If there are those of sharp faculties... then one may preach for them," the commentary says:
These sixty-six verses demonstrate the right and wrong of human conduct, enabling students to learn how to cultivate the former and abandon the latter.
This section contains four parts;
the first three have already been presented above. The fourth part, consisting of nineteen verses, should be explained to those who possess wisdom.
There are two parts:
first, seventeen verses that should explain the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and second, two verses that conclude them.
Within the first part, there are three sections:
The first one and a half verses may be taught to those who have never previously resolved their minds [for enlightenment], provided it can be verified that they possess the Buddha-lineage (*gotra*);
the next ten and a half verses may be taught to those who, although having already resolved their minds, have practiced the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*);
and the final five verses may be taught to those who, possessing both the innate nature and the practice, further possess a mind that reveres the Dharma and seeks the Dharma.
This first proof possesses six qualities:
first, keen faculties, because they understand quickly upon hearing;
second, wisdom, because they can distinguish between right and wrong.
Third is clarity of understanding, because one is not deluded or obscured.
Fourth is extensive learning, because one has previously cultivated the seeds of study.
Fifth is powerful memory, because one’s mental acuity is sharp and lucid.

Sixth, preach the Lotus Sūtra to those who delight in seeking the Buddha-way rather than other paths, who rejoice in transcending worldly dust, or whose nature seeks the path to awakening and who take no pleasure in folly and delusion; to such as these, it may be preached.
The Sūtra says: "If one has previously seen [the truth], only then may one preach it for them.
The Commentary states:
Although they have already generated the resolve and practiced the six perfections, [they are not yet ready].
Within this, there are six sections:

one and a half verses on the practice of having previously planted the habit of giving; one verse on the practice of diligence; one and a half verses on the practice of meditative concentration; three verses on the practice of ethical discipline; one and a half verses on the practice of patience; and two verses on the practice of wisdom.
This is the first [category].
Because they have previously seen a Buddha, they have long cultivated the habit of giving;
for them, one may explain it thus. Hereafter, whatever is verified shall be cited according to the matter, as investigated and explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
The Sūtra states: "If there is a person who is diligent, only then may [the teaching] be explained to them.
The commentary says:
The first verse praises diligence.
This one and a half verses concern the fixed [nature of the teaching].
The Sūtra says: “Furthermore, Śāriputra... only then may it be explained.
The Commentary states:
These three verses concern the practice of the precepts.
The first one and a half verses describe abandoning evil and drawing near to wholesome conditions; their characteristics will be explained in the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices" (*Anlehang pin*).
The latter one and a half verses concern the firm maintenance of pure precepts; the character "jie" (潔) is pronounced with the initial *gu* and the final *xie*, and it also means "pure."
Regarding the scripture passage, "If a person is without anger... then one may preach to them," the commentary states:
The first one and a half verses concern the cultivation of patience (*kṣānti*), while the latter two verses concern the cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*).
The patience of being upright and at ease with suffering; the patience of enduring enmity and harm out of constant compassion; and the patience of revering the Buddha and discerning the Dharma.
As the Sūtra says: "If there is a bhikṣu [who possesses these qualities], then one may preach this to him."
The commentary states:
The following five verses further demonstrate the seeking of the Dharma and the honoring of the Dharma.
This section is divided into two parts:
The first two and a half verses focus exclusively on seeking the Mahāyāna, while the latter two and a half verses emphasize earnestly seeking the Mahāyāna.
This initial section has two parts:
the first verse concerns receiving the Dharma upon the crown of the head, and the subsequent one and a half verses concern not seeking other sūtras.
"Other sūtras" refers to the sūtras of the Hīnayāna.
The *Śīla-samvara-sūtra* states:
"If one is studying the Mahāyāna internally but has not yet reached its ultimate consummation, one must not study other vehicles or other treatises on the four vidyās."
"If one is internally accomplished, one should study the Mahāyāna Abhidharma for two parts of each day, and study other sūtras for one part.
In this context, it is not permitted at all to study even a single verse of other sūtras, because beginners are required to seek [the Mahāyāna] exclusively;
those who have studied for a long time may practice both concurrently.
The Sūtra says: "As with a person who has reached the utmost sincerity, one may then preach for them.
The commentary states:
This clarifies the matter of earnest seeking.
There are two parts:
the first verse concerns earnest seeking, while the latter one and a half verses concern non-seeking.
One should not treat the external scriptures with disrespect; rather, only after one has abandoned the teachings of external paths may one preach to them.
Because "sincerity moves the gods" and "cultivating mindfulness makes one a sage," the Sūtra says, "He addressed Śāriputra... up to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The commentary states:
It should be explained to those who possess wisdom.
There are two [types of] *antarābhava*;
what has been presented above is the description of their characteristics, which now concludes the section.
